assumptions: The brief uses metric tonnes, so 1 tonne = 1,000 kg.
The stated shelter requests are treated as the accepted point demand estimates because no alternative accepted estimate or quantitative uncertainty model is supplied.
A trip may carry at most 0.6 t; the proposed allocation uses full 0.6 t loads.
Trips are modeled as nonnegative integers.
Crew-hours are consumed only by loading at the stated rate; no unloading, driving, standby, or inspection crew-hours are quantified in the brief.
The 12-hour horizon is treated as a dispatch requirement, but feasibility against travel and turnaround time cannot be established from the supplied data.
No rainfall demand multiplier is assumed because the brief supplies correlation but no causal study or quantitative relationship.

baseline.description: Simple proportional full-trip baseline: convert both demands to tonnes and divide the five crew-feasible trips in the 1.8:1.2 demand ratio.
evidence: The executable integer sanity case verified that (North trips, South trips) = (3,2) is feasible and exactly supplies both interpreted demands.
The baseline works here because each demand is an integer multiple of 0.6 t; it does not by itself generalize to non-aligned or uncertain demand.
baseline.result: North 3 trips (1.8 t), South 2 trips (1.2 t); 5 trips and 7.5 crew-hours.

candidate_models: Candidate A — proportional full-trip baseline: excellent fit for the supplied aligned demands, negligible implementation cost, but no explicit optimization machinery for shortages, uncertainty, or non-aligned demands; retained as the baseline, not the general selected formulation. Falsified as a general rule if proportional shares cannot be represented by feasible integer trips.

Candidate B — continuous linear allocation: variables are tonnes sent to each shelter; low implementation cost and supports shortage objectives, but it can hide indivisible trip decisions and therefore has weaker operational fit. Rejected because trips are explicitly counted and crew cost is per trip. It would be acceptable if partial trips and their crew accounting were explicitly authorized and modeled.

Candidate C — integer trip allocation: nonnegative integer trips by shelter with payload, trip, crew, and demand constraints; strong operational fit and low cost for two shelters. Selected because it represents the binding per-trip crew constraint and reproduces the exact allocation in an executable enumeration. Falsified if trips are not the relevant indivisible decision, if payload differs from 0.6 t, or if omitted travel/turnaround constraints make five trips impossible within 12 hours.

Candidate D — rainfall-adjusted robust/stochastic demand model: potentially useful for uncertainty, but the local brief provides neither a causal rainfall effect nor a distribution/scenario set. Rejected as unsupported and higher-cost. It may be reconsidered after an approved quantitative demand model and uncertainty data are supplied.
claims: Accepted conversion: North demand is 1.8 t and South demand is 1.2 t.
Provisional allocation: 3 full trips to North and 2 full trips to South.
The allocation exactly meets the accepted point demands and satisfies the stated trip and loading-crew constraints.
The crew-hour limit is binding and permits at most five loaded trips.
Rainfall is relevant context for uncertainty but does not support a numerical demand adjustment from the supplied evidence.
The executable integer-scaled sanity case verified the mathematical allocation; it did not validate real-world dispatch feasibility.
No dispatch approval or physical validation is claimed.

data_findings: The requests align exactly with full truckloads: North requires 3 loads and South requires 2 loads.
The crew constraint, not the stated six-trip availability, is binding.
The feasible exact-demand allocation uses all capacity permitted by the crew constraint, leaving 0.5 crew-hours and one nominal trip unused.
No numerical uncertainty interval, rainfall-response coefficient, attendance series, pack weight/count, route duration, unloading requirement, road status, or safety threshold is provided.
Because no spare crew-supported payload remains, any positive demand uplift cannot be carried under the stated loading-resource constraint without changing resources or assumptions.

The first executable sanity check used binary floating-point equality and returned no exact allocation despite the mathematically exact solution; an integer-tenths formulation removed that numerical artifact.
experiment_design: Use the local brief as the sole problem-data source and normalize all mass values to tonnes.
Establish a simple proportional baseline before selecting a model.
Compare continuous, integer, and rainfall-adjusted formulations on structural fit, evidence needs, implementation cost, and falsification conditions.
Enumerate the small integer decision space as the minimal executable sanity case.

For operational validation, independently weigh or count sealed packs per load, reconcile totals to the manifest, confirm crew and truck availability, confirm destination acceptance, check route/weather safety, and obtain dispatch authorization.

Sensitivity checks should vary available crew, per-trip labor, payload, and accepted demand; rainfall-driven demand must not be varied quantitatively until an approved relationship or scenario set exists.
falsification_tests: If 1 tonne is not intended to mean 1,000 kg, reject the conversion and recompute Task 2.
If either stated request is not the accepted demand estimate, reject the allocation and rerun the model with the approved values.
If usable payload is below 0.6 t, five trips cannot deliver the full 3.0 t and the solution is falsified.
If loading requires more than 1.6 crew-hours per trip, five trips exceed 8 crew-hours; the proposed exact allocation is infeasible.
If fewer than 7.5 loading crew-hours or fewer than five trips are actually available, reject the allocation.
If five trips cannot be completed in 12 hours because of travel, turnaround, or weather constraints, reject the operational plan.
If rainfall is assigned a quantitative demand effect without an approved causal or scenario model, reject that adjustment as unsupported.
If pack sizes prevent exact 600 kg loads or exact shelter totals, revise the discrete formulation using pack counts.

constraints: n_N and n_S are nonnegative integers.
For the proposed full-load allocation: q_N = 0.6 n_N and q_S = 0.6 n_S.
Rainfall is not a decision variable and no unsupported causal demand constraint is introduced.
notes: The selected formulation is a planning model, not dispatch authorization.
Integer tenths of a tonne were used in the executable exactness check to avoid binary floating-point equality errors.
The rainfall parameter is retained for traceability but has no numerical demand effect without further evidence.
formalization.objective: Lexicographically minimize total unmet demand d_N + d_S, then minimize dispatched trips; under the supplied parameters the zero-shortage solution is n_N = 3 and n_S = 2.
parameters: R = 75 mm rainfall forecast; recorded as a non-controllable contextual parameter with no accepted response coefficient.
units: Mass is normalized to metric tonnes: 1,800 kg = 1.8 t; 1.2 t = 1,200 kg.
Truck capacity is 0.6 t/trip, equal to 600 kg/trip.
Labor is measured in crew-hours; loading uses 1.5 crew-hours/trip.
Time horizon is measured in hours.
One-row unit summary: North demand 1.8 t | South demand 1.2 t | total demand 3.0 t | payload 0.6 t/trip | allocation 3 + 2 trips | delivered 1.8 + 1.2 t | crew 7.5 crew-hours | rainfall 75 mm.
variables: n_N: integer number of trips assigned to Shelter North.
n_S: integer number of trips assigned to Shelter South.
q_N: tonnes allocated to Shelter North.
q_S: tonnes allocated to Shelter South.
d_N and d_S: unmet demand in tonnes, used if an exact allocation is infeasible.

human_gates: A responsible planner must confirm that the stated requests are the accepted demand estimates and approve the metric-tonne conversion.
Operations staff must verify pack manifests, payload, vehicle readiness, crew schedule, route safety, travel timing, and shelter receipt capability.
A qualified decision-maker must decide whether additional rainfall-related demand scenarios are required; none are inferred here.
Dispatch authorization is required after validation. This approval is absent, so the proposed allocation must not be treated as authorized or FINAL.
reality_constraints: The allocation covers the next 12 hours.
North requests 1,800 kg, equal to 1.8 t.
South requests 1.2 t, equal to 1,200 kg.
Total interpreted demand is 3.0 t, equal to 3,000 kg.
Truck payload is bounded by 0.6 t per trip.
No more than six trips are available.
Total loading labor is bounded by 8 crew-hours, limiting dispatch to floor(8/1.5) = 5 loaded trips.
Five full trips carry at most 3.0 t and consume 7.5 crew-hours.
Six loaded trips would consume 9 crew-hours and violate the crew constraint.
Rainfall is fixed at the forecast value of 75 mm for this decision and is not controllable.
Historical attendance-rainfall correlation does not establish a causal demand adjustment.
requirements: Task 1: trace requirements and identify controllable decisions.

Task 1 input: North request 1,800 kg; South request 1.2 tonnes; truck capacity 0.6 tonnes per trip; six trips available; loading cost 1.5 crew-hours per trip; at most 8 crew-hours; rainfall forecast 75 mm.
Task 1 output: an accepted demand interpretation and unit conversion that Task 2 must use.
Task 1 controllable decisions: trips dispatched to each shelter, load assigned to each trip, and whether dispatch is authorized after validation.
Task 1 evaluation: conversions must be dimensionally consistent and identified constraints must be traceable to local evidence.
Task 2: propose an allocation using Task 1's accepted conversion and demand interpretation.
Task 2 output: allocate 3 full trips (1.8 t) to North and 2 full trips (1.2 t) to South; total 5 trips, 3.0 t, and 7.5 crew-hours.
Task 2 evaluation: meet both accepted demands without exceeding truck capacity, six available trips, or 8 crew-hours.
Task 2 dependency: the allocation is valid only under Task 1's interpretation that the stated requests are the accepted demand estimates and 1 tonne = 1,000 kg.
Task 3 output: a pre-dispatch checklist covering physical load, resource, destination, weather/route, and authorization checks.
Task 3 evaluation: dispatch remains blocked until required facts are checked and a responsible human approves it.
Final handoff requirement: include a one-row unit summary even if no model is selected.
robustness_tests: Crew availability: the plan is feasible at 7.5 crew-hours and has a 0.5 crew-hour margin; any availability below 7.5 is infeasible for five trips.
Loading-time sensitivity: the largest feasible rate for five trips is 8/5 = 1.6 crew-hours per trip, leaving a margin of 0.1 crew-hour per trip over the stated 1.5.
Payload sensitivity: exact total delivery in five trips requires an average 0.6 t per trip, so there is no payload-downside margin.
Demand sensitivity: there is no crew-supported spare payload under the full-load assumption; any positive total demand uplift creates shortage unless resources or loading assumptions change.
Trip availability: reducing availability from six to five has no effect; reducing it below five makes the exact allocation infeasible.
Rainfall robustness is unresolved because no quantitative uncertainty relation or approved scenarios are supplied.
selected_model: Candidate C — integer trip allocation, used provisionally for planning; dispatch still requires the stated human gate.
self_reported_limitations: Only the listed local files and local command outputs were used; no external evidence was consulted.
The task was analyzed as a one-time observation and no design or implementation-plan files were created.
The selected model covers allocation and loading labor but cannot prove five-trip completion within 12 hours without route and turnaround data.
No causal or statistical rainfall-demand model can be estimated from the supplied correlation statement.
No physical inventory, vehicle, crew, route, shelter, or human-approval validation was possible in the repository.
The initial binary floating-point equality test was numerically unsuitable; its failure and the corrected integer-scaled result are both disclosed.

validation: Arithmetic validation: 3 × 0.6 t = 1.8 t for North and 2 × 0.6 t = 1.2 t for South.
Demand validation: total proposed delivery is 3.0 t, equal to the total accepted point demand.
Before dispatch, verify actual pack mass/count and seals against a signed manifest; the brief does not provide pack-level data.
Before dispatch, verify truck payload rating, mechanical readiness, crew availability, and that 7.5 loading crew-hours are actually schedulable.
Before dispatch, verify routes and turnaround times permit five trips within 12 hours, especially under the 75 mm forecast.
Before dispatch, confirm both shelters can receive the stated quantities and record a responsible human's approval.
Any failed physical, timing, safety, demand-acceptance, or authorization check reopens the earliest affected conversion, resource, or model decision and blocks dispatch.
